props.title: You Can't Take It with You
props.initialSlug: Eccentric family teaches banker about life's true riches

sections.content: Frank Capra's adaptation of the Kaufman-Hart play **You Can't Take It with You** (1938) represents the pinnacle of Depression-era optimistic filmmaking. Starring Jean Arthur and James Stewart, this Best Picture winner masterfully blends screwball comedy with social commentary about American values. Like Capra's other classics **Mr. Smith Goes to Washington** (1939) and **It's a Wonderful Life** (1946), the film champions individualism and free-spirited nonconformity against soulless corporate greed. The eccentric Vanderhof family embodies the director's idealistic vision of American democracy - a harmonious chaos of personal passions and artistic pursuits.

sections.content: The film's influence resonates through later comedy-dramas about eccentric families, from **The Royal Tenenbaums** (2001) to **Little Miss Sunshine** (2006). Lionel Barrymore's performance as Grandpa Vanderhof established the archetype of the wise family patriarch who chooses happiness over wealth - a character type that would influence countless films about resisting materialism. The romance between Arthur and Stewart also set a template for stories about young lovers bridging class divides, seen later in films like **Pretty in Pink** (1986) and **Notting Hill** (1999).

The technical achievement shouldn't be overlooked - the film's elaborate mansion set allowed Capra to stage complex scenes with up to 30 actors simultaneously, creating a choreographed chaos that influenced later ensemble comedies. The cinematography by Joseph Walker captures both intimate moments and grand setpieces with equal skill, establishing visual patterns that would become hallmarks of American comedy. sections.content: Released during the latter years of the Great Depression, **You Can't Take It with You** (1938) resonated deeply with audiences through its criticism of ruthless capitalism while avoiding bitter cynicism. Unlike grittier Depression films like **I Am a Fugitive from a Chain Gang** (1932), Capra's approach emphasized hope and human connection. This optimistic but socially conscious style influenced later filmmakers like Preston Sturges in **Sullivan's Travels** (1941) and Frank Darabont in **The Shawshank Redemption** (1994).
